title: POC Weekly Sync - Dedicated Sizing & Autoscaling
summary: Weekly POC check-in focused on Dedicated sizing, autoscaling policies and burst capacity planning. Reviewed last week's benchmark results, discussed p95 latency targets, KV cache hit rates, and trade-offs between pre-warmed capacity vs burstable pools. Action items: Redwood to share updated Dedicated pricing and autoscaling proposal, customer to run 24h mixed-workload load test and confirm peak windows.

transcript:
Header: 2026-02-23 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~45 min | Attendees: Samir Patel, Lina Wu, Diego Ramos / Mark Reynolds, Priya Shah, Jordan Miller, Erin Cole

Optional auto-summary: quick sync after last week's smoke runs; focus on capacity planning for Dedicated pilot and autoscaler tuning.

00:00 Samir Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick check — is this still a good time?
00:06 Mark Reynolds: Yeah, all good here. Priya and Jordan are on.
00:08 Priya Shah: Yep, hi.
00:10 Samir Patel: Cool. Lina, want to kick off with the benchmark highlights you pulled?
00:15 Lina Wu: Sure. So we re-ran the mixed workload from last Friday — small chat, long-form generation, and embeddings. I have the numbers up front: median latency for short prompts is ~120ms, p95 is about 380ms on the pre-warmed nodes; embeddings stayed around 45ms. We saw KV cache hit rates around 72% after warm-up, but one thing to flag is a drop to ~48% when we simulated cold-starts.
00:45 Jordan Miller: That cold-start drop is the one that worries us — our busiest window has lots of infrequent sessions, so burst will matter.
00:52 Lina Wu: Right, which is where the burst pool and autoscaler policy come in — you can set a smaller baseline of pre-warmed GPUs and allow for an on-demand burst pool that can spin up additional instances. The tradeoff is cost vs the p95 SLA during those bursts.
01:10 Samir Patel: To add, Redwood Dedicated supports a few approaches: (1) higher min nodes to keep p95 low, (2) lower min with a fast burst (if you accept a short degradation), or (3) hybrid where we keep a small warm pool + very short lived micro-burst VMs for extreme spikes.
01:28 Priya Shah: Can you quantify "short degradation"? We need to know how long a spin-up is and whether queueing will buffer requests.
01:35 Lina Wu: Spin-up time we measured on the cluster is roughly 20–40 seconds to get a new GPU node ready and the runtime warmed, plus another ~5–10s for the KV cache to repopulate for that instance. Queueing can be enabled — Redwood will queue incoming requests up to a configured limit; beyond that you get 429/overload handling or fallback to hosted models if you enable fallback.
01:58 Mark Reynolds: Hmm. For Novella, 20–40s is okay if we have graceful degradation, but not if user-facing workflows time out. We do have a server-side retry on our side for non-blocking flows.
02:08 Samir Patel: Good input. For the pilot, we should align on target SLOs. Priya, Jordan, what are your p95 targets during peak?
02:16 Priya Shah: Ideally <500ms for short-chat p95. For long-form generation it's less strict — we aim for <2.5s p95.
02:24 Jordan Miller: On throughput, our current QPS at peak is ~18 concurrent requests that decode to ~12k tokens per minute on average per second — apologies, that is messy — basically ~200 tpm (tokens per minute?) no, let me rephrase — about 12k tokens per minute across the cluster, which becomes ~200 tokens/sec sustained, with bursts up to ~700 tokens/sec.
02:46 Lina Wu: Got it. That maps to roughly X GPUs depending on model and quantization. For the 7B-ish model you're running in the POC, we estimate ~1 GPU can handle ~250 tokens/sec with batching, but that's sensitive to prompt length and KV cache hit rate. With your burst of 700 tokens/sec, we'd recommend baseline 2 GPUs with 1-2 GPU burst capacity.
03:10 Mark Reynolds: Can you remind me of the exact model variant you used in the test? I think one of the model names got munged in the last transcript.
03:16 Lina Wu: Yeah, we used the redwood-rev7b q4 variant — i might have noted it as rev7k earlier in the doc, apologies. It's the quantized 7B profile.
03:24 Erin Cole: Any cost estimates for baseline vs burst?
03:27 Samir Patel: I'll share an updated pricing sheet, but ballpark: baseline dedicated nodes at 2x A10-equivalent GPUs with reserved commit will be more cost-effective than purely burstable on-demand; burst tiers priced per-hourly and per-GB of bandwidth for model weights warm. We'll provide two price scenarios in the doc: aggressive warm pool vs lean warm pool + burst.
03:50 Priya Shah: On security, quick question: does Dedicated support customer-managed KMS? We need to ensure keys never leave our control.
03:57 Diego Ramos: Yes — Dedicated private deployments can integrate with your KMS (we've done AWS KMS and some HSM partners). For VPC and private control plane, logs and audit can be pushed to your cloud log bucket or forwarded to your SIEM. We'll attach the SOC2 + ISO section in the security doc.
04:15 Mark Reynolds: Good. Also related — how are access controls handled between engineers and data scientists? We need RBAC so some users can't download model snapshots.
04:22 Samir Patel: RBAC is supported in the Console with role templates; we can map SAML groups to roles. We'll include the role mapping guide.
04:30 Jordan Miller: Back to autoscaler config — what's the recommended cooldown and scale step? We saw a lot of oscillation in earlier tests.
04:37 Lina Wu: Our typical recommendation: scale step of 1 node, cooldown 120–180s, and use a multi-metric policy (CPU/GPU utilization + queue length + p95 latency). Also enable a short warm-up prefetch — when we detect predicted traffic increase (based on historical windows) we pre-warm an extra node 60s before. That reduces cold-start pain.
05:02 Priya Shah: How does pre-warm prediction work? Is it rule-based or ML?
05:05 Lina Wu: Right now it's rule-based with heuristics we can tune for your use-case; we also offer hooks to your telemetry so we can do scheduled window pre-warms.
05:14 Mark Reynolds: For the POC we want a conservative default that won't cost us too much but keeps user-facing calls within p95 < 500ms. So baseline 2 nodes, burst to 4, with 2-node pre-warm? Thoughts?
05:28 Lina Wu: That seems reasonable. Baseline of 2 nodes and a max of 4 with a burst pool we can cap at 2. Keep cooldowns 2 minutes, scale step 1. We'll simulate that in a runbook and show expected p95 distributions.
05:40 Jordan Miller: Can you show expected latency curves for those settings? The earlier spreadsheet had median but not distribution.
05:47 Lina Wu: Yes, we'll regenerate the chart using the new policy. Expect p95 to stay <500ms in most cases, but during cold bursts we could see a spike to ~900–1.2s for the first few requests unless queueing is active.
06:05 Priya Shah: Okay, that spike is acceptable for non-interactive tasks but not for patient-facing chat. We'll probably set fallback to hosted model for those flows so UX stays snappy.
06:15 Samir Patel: Good hybrid approach. We'll document the fallback route and how to configure it in the Console.
06:20 Mark Reynolds: Another item — KV cache miss behavior. We saw cold misses cause longer decode times. Is there a way to pre-warm KV cache across nodes?
06:27 Lina Wu: We have a prefix caching option where you can populate common prompts ahead of time; also sticky routing can help keep sessions on warmed nodes. For multi-node bursts, there's no global instant KV sync — we rely on either repopulation or a shared cold-cache layer which we can enable at a small cost.
06:46 Priya Shah: What's the small cost?
06:48 Samir Patel: We'll quantify it in the pricing doc, likely a small throughput+storage delta.
06:53 Jordan Miller: Regarding metrics, can you emit per-token cost and P95 per-route in the Console? We want to attribute costs to product features.
07:00 Diego Ramos: Yes, Console provides per-route token breakdowns, and you can tag routes to visualize cost per feature.
07:06 Erin Cole: Great. Next — runbook for incidents: if one GPU fails during peak what happens?
07:11 Lina Wu: The runtime re-routes to remaining GPUs and autoscaler tries to replace the node; if you're at min capacity you might see increased latency. We can set automatic fallback to hosted or to a lower-cost model as a safety valve.
07:25 Priya Shah: Do you have SLA language for Dedicated in pilot?
07:28 Samir Patel: For pilots we can't promise full enterprise SLA, but we'll provide operational support and 4-hour incident response from our on-call. For Dedicated contracts we include 99.x% uptime SLAs. We'll include the pilot support terms in the follow-up email.
07:41 Mark Reynolds: Sounds good. Any surprises from the logs we should know?
07:44 Lina Wu: One thing — we saw some tokenization anomalies where a few prompts caused decode slowdowns; we traced it to very long context windows and a mis-specified chunking parameter in the client. Jordan's team fixed that but we'll share the note.
08:00 Jordan Miller: Yep, that was on us — fixed the chunk size. The next run looks cleaner.
08:06 Samir Patel: OK moving to next steps — we'll run a 24h mixed workload test with scheduled peaks to validate the autoscaler and burst plan. Priya, Jordan you run that and upload logs. Lina and Diego will set up the runbook and expected output.
08:21 Priya Shah: We'll do it this Friday; uploading by Monday.
08:24 Samir Patel: Great. Lina, can you also share an adjusted spreadsheet with cost scenarios for the two baseline options?
08:29 Lina Wu: Yup, will send it today.
08:31 Mark Reynolds: On timeline — after the 24h run, is there an easy path to convert to Dedicated reserved for production?
08:36 Samir Patel: Yes — pilot -> reserved commit is straightforward. We'll propose a commit level based on observed sustained throughput and a buy-down pricing for reserved capacity. We'll include transition steps in the doc.
08:45 Erin Cole: One compliance question — will audit logs include per-request metadata for our internal auditors?
08:50 Diego Ramos: Yes, we can produce audit logs with request IDs, user IDs, timestamps; PII masking can be applied prior to logs leaving your environment if needed.
08:58 Mark Reynolds: Awesome. Anything else?
09:00 Samir Patel: Quick recap of next actions: Samir to send pricing + security docs; Lina to send KV-cache tuning and new latency curves; Priya/Jordan to run load tests and share logs; Diego to attach SOC2 and KMS integration notes. We'll reconvene after the 24h run to review.
09:17 Priya Shah: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
09:20 Samir Patel: Thanks all. We'll send notes and schedule the benchmark follow-up.
09:25 Mark Reynolds: Bye.

End of transcript. Some transcription artifacts present: 'rev7k' for rev7b earlier, 'K V cash' spelled out in one spot. Couple of short overlaps and filler words retained.
